newsitem.title: UK: Labour's tax-raising first budget fails to please.
newsitem.headline: Labour's tax-raising first budget fails to please.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government unveiled a tax-raising first budget, pledging to create 250,000 new jobs and boost spending on schools and hospitals, while slashing the budget deficit.

Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown said the first Labour budget since 1978 contained a net fiscal tightening of 5.5 billion pounds ($9.1 billion) this year -- 0.5 percent of gross domestic product -- and 4.75 billion next.
But financial markets complained that Brown had not done nearly enough to dampen soaring consumer spending and therefore made steep interest rate rises inevitable.
"The corporate sector gets hit by a triple whammy," said Douglas McWilliams, head of the Centre for Economics and Business Research.
"Net corporate tax payments will go up, companies will have to pay higher interest rates and they face higher exchange rates. It's a tough outlook for the corporate sector."
The centrepiece of the budget was, as expected, a "welfare-to-work" programme to create jobs for 250,000 young people.

This will be financed by a one-off tax on the profits of utility companies privatised by the former Conservative government, which will yield around 5.2 billion pounds -- at the upper end of market expectations.
Brown also scrapped a tax credit on dividend payments, but tried to sweeten the pill by reducing corporation tax to 31 percent from 33 percent.
There was a gesture in the direction of "green" taxes in the former of lower excise duties on buses and trucks and a pledge to examine the case for making polluters pay.
Environmental groups dismissed this as no more than a modest step in the right direction, which would do little to change people's behaviour.

But apart from dearer petrol, cigarettes and alcohol, all consumers had to worry about was a cut in tax relief on mortgage interest payments and an increase in stamp duty on houses at the top end of the property market.

"The promise of a radical budget to rebalance the economy by squeezing consumer spending and encouraging investment has not been backed up by the measures announced by Gordon Brown," said Andrew Sentance of the London Business School.
"When we look in detail at the budget arithmetic, the impact on the consumer is pretty modest."

The Bank of England, which was empowered by Brown to set interest rates in his most radical move as Chancellor, issued a diplomatic statement saying the budget helped "to address the policy dilemma we are confronted with."
But economists were virtually unanimous in predicting that the Bank would act again soon -- possibly as early as next week -- to raise interest rates from their present 6.5 percent.

It fears strong consumer spending, fuelled in particular by around 30 billion pounds of "windfall" gains for consumers as mutually owned building societies turn themselves into banks, will result in inflation unless it is curbed through higher rates.
The dilemma for the authorities is that higher interest rates will almost inevitably boost the pound even further, making life more difficult for the country's already struggling exporters.
"This budget has left the economy open to many shocks," said Gerard Lyons, an economist at DKB International. "As a result of those potential shocks, interest rates are likely to go higher."

"The Bank of England, the financial markets, international investors wanted the Chancellor to cool the economy by hitting the consumer. But you are not going to get balanced growth solely by the fiscal measures announced this afternoon."
McWilliams sees official interest rates at around 8.0 percent by the middle of next year, a view shared by Andrew Milligan, an economist at General Accident.
"Brown has put a very light foot on the brakes, not enough to slow the economy quickly," Milligan said.
($ = 0.602 British Pounds)
